content:
Lists of complaints about Islam and women tend to bundle these rules together: the testimony of two women for one man, the smaller inheritance share, polygamy, honour killing, genital cutting and a husband's claim on his wife. The first three come from the Quran. Honour killing and genital cutting are customs that the texts do not support, and the last point concerns a hadith often misread.

Each point below states the objection at full strength and then reads the relevant text with its classical interpretation.

The bundling matters because it hides the difference between what the texts command and what some societies do. A reader who meets all six in one list may assume they rest on one authority. Some are Quranic rules with a stated purpose, some are customs that predate Islam and survive in parts of the Muslim world and beyond it, and one is a report whose meaning has been stretched. Separating them is the first step to judging any of them fairly.

The objection runs as follows: the Quran itself rates a woman's word at half a man's, since a debt needs two male witnesses or one man and two women. The verse exists and says this. It sets out how to record a loan, and asks for two men, or one man and two women, so that if one of the women forgets, the other may remind her.[1]

Its scope is narrow. Taha Jabir al-Alwani observed that this is the only verse in the Quran that pairs two women with one man, and that most jurists classed much of its content as guidance on avoiding disputes over money, with only a few treating it as binding.[2] The verse gives its own reason, the risk that one witness forgets, which al-Alwani tied to a society in which women seldom handled credit.[2]

The classical schools did not apply the ratio across the board. Ibn Rushd, in his comparative manual of the schools, records agreement that property is established by one man and two women on the strength of the verse, and that the majority accepted the testimony of women alone, with no man present, in matters that men seldom witness, such as childbirth, the cry of a newborn and women's hidden defects.[3] The schools differed on the number required for such testimony: Malik held that two women suffice, al-Shafi'i held four, and Abu Hanifa accepted a woman's word for what lies between the navel and the knee.[3] He adds that the schools also discussed the testimony of a single woman to a case of suckling, in light of the Prophet's question to the man in the report, "How, when she has suckled you both?"[3]

Ibn al-Qayyim went further. He argued that the verse on debts teaches the creditor how to secure his right in writing and witnesses, and that it does not limit what a judge may accept as proof. In court, he wrote, the test is whatever makes the truth clear, and a judge may rule on the testimony of a woman where it does so.[4]

The hadith scholars applied no ratio at all. A report narrated by a single woman was accepted on the same terms as one narrated by a single man, and a great part of the law rests on reports from A'isha alone. Al-Dhahabi, who compiled a vast dictionary of weak and disputed narrators, remarked that he knew of no woman among them who had been accused of lying.[5] In the transmission of religion itself, the most consequential testimony of all, a woman's word counted as a man's.

Critics point to the rule that a son receives twice the share of a daughter.[6] That rule is part of a wider system. The same chapter of the Quran makes the husband responsible for supporting his wife from his own wealth,[7] and requires that the bride receive her dowry (mahr, the marriage gift) as her own property, which she may waive only by her own choice.[8]

A daughter keeps what she inherits and what she receives at marriage, and owes nothing to the household. Her brother carries the cost of a wife, children and, in classical law, needy relatives. The double share funds a duty that she does not bear. The two-to-one ratio also holds in only some cases: a mother and father each receive one sixth from a child who leaves offspring, an equal share.[6]

Other rules in the same chapter give men and women equal shares. Brothers and sisters through the mother inherit equally, each taking a sixth, or sharing a third if there are more of them.[9] In some combinations of heirs a daughter or a sister receives more than a male relative of a more distant degree. The system is built on degrees of kinship and on the duties attached to them, and the two-to-one rule is one result of it.

The law also leaves room for choice. A person may bequeath up to a third of the estate to those who are not fixed heirs, a limit the Prophet set when Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas asked whether he could give away more, telling him that a third is much.[10] Parents may also give gifts in their lifetime. Many Muslim families have used these provisions to help a daughter whose circumstances require it.

The verse that allows a man up to four wives at once attaches a condition in the same sentence: if he fears that he will not be just, then one.[11] A later verse in the same chapter tells men that they will never be able to deal with their wives with full equality however much they wish to, and forbids them to leave a wife suspended.[12]

Read together, the verses set a ceiling and a test of justice that the Quran itself says few men will pass in full. The text names one wife as the course for a man who doubts that he can be fair.

The verse was a limit when it was revealed. Before Islam a man in Arabia might keep any number of wives. When Ghaylan ibn Salama embraced Islam with ten wives, the Prophet told him to keep four and part from the rest.[13] The Quran placed a ceiling on an existing practice and attached to it a condition of justice.

Classical law also gave the wife a means of protection. In the Hanbali school, a woman may stipulate in her marriage contract that her husband will not take a second wife, and if he breaks the condition she may dissolve the marriage.[14] Several modern Muslim states have written versions of that rule into their family law, and others require a court's permission before a second marriage.

Honour killing is often presented as an Islamic practice. The clearest report on the question points the other way. Sa'd ibn Ubada asked the Prophet whether a man who found another man with his wife should kill him. The Prophet answered no.[15] When Sa'd protested, the Prophet told those present to listen to what their chief was saying drawing attention to his outburst. The answer to the question itself stood: no.[15]

Islamic law treats the accusation of adultery as a matter for a court, with a demanding standard of proof and a separate procedure of mutual oaths (li'an) for a husband who has no witnesses. Private vengeance has no place in that scheme.

The Quran sets out that procedure in Surat al-Nur. A husband who accuses his wife without four witnesses swears four times by God that he is truthful and a fifth time that the curse of God be upon him if he lies; the wife averts the punishment by swearing four times that he lies and a fifth time that the wrath of God be upon her if he tells the truth.[16] The marriage ends and neither is punished. The law's answer to a husband's suspicion is an oath before a judge, which protects the wife from his anger as much as from a false charge.

Defenders of the practice cite one report, in which the Prophet told a woman who performed circumcision in Medina not to cut severely. Abu Dawud, who recorded it, judged it himself: he called it a weak report, noted that it was also transmitted with a gap in its chain, and said that one of its narrators is unknown.[17]

In November 2006 the Grand Imam of al-Azhar, Muhammad Sayyid Tantawi, said that he found nothing in religion requiring circumcision for women, and the Grand Mufti of Egypt, Ali Gomaa, noted that the Prophet did not circumcise his daughters.[18]

The practice is far older than Islam and is found among Christians and followers of traditional religions in parts of Africa, while it is unknown in most of the Muslim world, including much of the Arabian Peninsula, Turkey, Iran and South Asia. That geography shows a regional custom, and it explains why scholars who examined the texts could find no religious basis for it. The prohibition of harm, a principle the jurists drew from the Prophet's words "no harm and no harming", weighs against any practice that injures the body without benefit.

Critics say that Islamic law grants a husband sex on demand, and cite the report that if a man calls his wife to bed and she refuses, so that he spends the night angry, the angels curse her until morning.[19] The report is a moral warning addressed to the wife about refusal that leaves her husband aggrieved. It describes the husband going to sleep angry. It prescribes no penalty and grants him no licence to compel her.

The Quran frames the marriage bond in other terms. Spouses are a garment for one another.[20] God placed affection and mercy between them so that each may find rest in the other.[21] Husbands are commanded to live with their wives on a footing of kindness (bi al-ma'ruf, according to what is right and decent).[22] Force against a wife breaks each of these commands, and the jurists' ban on harm, cited in the article on 4:34, applies to it.

The law protects the woman's consent at the start of the marriage as well. Khansa bint Khidham was married by her father to a man she did not want, and she went to the Prophet, who annulled the marriage.[23] The Prophet also said that a previously married woman is not given in marriage without being consulted, and a virgin not without her permission.[24] A marriage that begins with her consent and is governed by kindness leaves no place for compulsion within it.

The bottom line

The rules on testimony, inheritance and polygamy are in the Quran, and each comes with a stated purpose and a limit: testimony in loans with the risk of forgetting, inheritance with the duty of support, polygamy with the condition of justice. The jurists applied them within those limits and debated their scope. Honour killing and female genital cutting have no sound basis in the texts, and the Prophet refused a husband the right to kill. The hadith on intimacy is a moral warning to a wife, set within a marriage the Quran describes in terms of affection and mercy.

A fair judgement of Islamic law on women weighs each rule with its reason and its context. Some readers will still disagree with the result, and that is a legitimate debate. It is a different debate from the one the bundled list suggests.
